title: Krishna and Balarama Slay the Wrestlers
story:
Kamsa, the king of Mathura, had called the brothers to a festival of arms, and everyone in the packed arena understood what the invitation meant: the king had spent years trying to destroy these two boys, and today he meant to do it openly. Krishna and Balarama had come from the cowherds' village across the Yamuna because a king's word is a command, and now they stood in the great ring while Kamsa set his champions against them. Chanura and Mushtika were not ordinary men. They were wrestlers hardened in every limb, and the two who faced them were boys, barely arrived in the city, soft-faced and bright-eyed. The crowd saw the mismatch the moment it was announced. There was nothing festive about the day, and no one dared say the truth aloud until the match was under way.

Then the match began, and it was stranger than anyone expected. Hand to hand and foot to foot the four of them gripped, whirling and throwing and grappling, lifting and shaking and dropping, each reading the other's strength. Skill answered skill, though the bodies could not have been more unequal. The women of the assembly could not keep silent. "What injustice is this," they cried toward the royal seats, "for these honored ones? The wrestlers are hard as diamond in every limb, like mountains — and look at the faces of these two boys! Do you not see Krishna's lotus face as he moves about his enemy, and Balarama's eyes gone red? Fortunate is the land of Vraja, where such boys grew up tending cows and playing the flute, garlands of wild flowers in their hair. What penance did the cowherd women of that village perform, that they might see such a face at the morning milking and at the evening homecoming?" But the fight went on, for the king had willed it, and the wrestlers, hearing the women's fear, only pressed in harder.

Krishna heard them, and something in him answered their concern. He sprang at Chanura with both fists clenched and struck — and the blow landed the way a garland lands on an elephant, light and unregarded. But he did not break off. He seized the great wrestler, whirled him through the air, and dashed him to the ground, and Chanura's life left him there in the dust of the arena.

Beside him, Balarama met Mushtika, and his fist found its mark until Mushtika sagged and fell. The other champions came forward then, one after another, and the brothers dealt with them the same way: Kuta went down before Balarama, Shala fell to a blow from Krishna's foot, and Tośala after them, until not one of the king's wrestlers was left standing.

The assembly sat stunned. This was not the sport Kamsa had promised. Two boys had walked into an arena built to break them and had walked out untouched, while the men who were meant to break them lay still. The brothers stood in the middle of the ring, breathing easily, as though the morning had cost them nothing. The women who had cried out against the injustice did not cheer; they had simply been proved right. High on his dais, the king who had arranged all of it sat very still.
reflection: The women's protest is the moral heart of the scene: the crowd recognizes the injustice before the fight is decided, and says so aloud. Their outcry does not stop the contest, but it records for the reader exactly who understood the truth of what was being arranged.
content_note: The death of the wrestlers is described briefly; the Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana give a more graphic account than the Bhagavata, which this telling follows.
next_story_tease: But the king's fury was not spent — the death of his champions only stoked it.
hero_scene: In the crowded Mathura arena, Krishna — small against a wrestler like a mountain — whirls Chanura through the air by the limbs, preparing to dash him down, while the women in the stands rise in protest and Balarama grapples with Mushtika.
visual_elements: the women of the assembly rising in protest
